strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: discovering instance-specific, unsupervised symmetry distributions rather than dataset-level or fixed symmetries is a meaningful and underexplored problem in equivariant learning.

The core idea is elegant and technically sound: using the Fréchet mean to normalize the arbitrary canonical pose offset from class-pose decompositions (IE-AEs) is a simple but principled fix, and Proposition 3.1 with the accompanying proof (Appendix B) provides reasonable theoretical justification with convergence in Wasserstein distance.

The paper addresses a real limitation of prior work (SGMs and IE-AEs learn distributions relative to arbitrary canonicals), and the 6-vs-9 partial symmetry example concretely demonstrates where full equivariance fails and where RECON helps.

First demonstration of unsupervised symmetry distribution discovery for 3D transformation groups (SO(3)) on large-scale molecular data (GEOM/QM9, ~220k samples, 2,221 classes), which extends beyond the typical 2D benchmarks.
Practical downstream application (OOD pose detection with AUC-ROC of 0.92/0.80/0.75) shows the learned distributions have utility beyond analysis.
Good reproducibility: code is released, and the appendix contains detailed architectures, hyperparameters, data preparation, and training schedules for all experiments.
Honest limitations section that discusses failure modes (non-trivial errors for a minority of molecules) and future directions.
weaknesses: Limited quantitative comparison against baselines. The main baselines (SGM, IE-AE, SGM-style methods) are mostly compared qualitatively (Figures 4, 5) or via qualitative discussion; there is no head-to-head quantitative symmetry-recovery metric reported for competing methods, making it hard to judge how much better RECON is rather than merely different.

The theoretical result relies on assumptions that are strong and not verified in practice: ψ continuous on a compact domain, noise bounded almost surely by ε', uniqueness of the Fréchet mean within radius r0, and exact class membership via an ε-connected equivalence relation. The actual algorithm uses k-NN approximation of classes, deviating from the theory without formal justification of when this is valid.

The 'real-world' 3D claim is partially overstated: the ground-truth SO(3) symmetry distributions in GEOM are synthetic matrix-Fisher distributions applied by the authors, not naturally occurring symmetries; the method thus recovers injected ground truth rather than discovered natural symmetries.

Evaluation on molecules has a substantial failure region: roughly 20% of molecules have MSE > 800, and the explanation ('other sources such as limited conformer sampling or mixed symmetries') is speculative; the MSE between matrix-Fisher parameters is also a somewhat ad hoc metric without analysis of what error levels are practically meaningful.

Method inherits the quality of the underlying IE-AE: the assumption that structurally similar objects map to nearby points in the invariant space (Equation 1) is asserted empirically rather than guaranteed, and classes with multiple modes, continuous shape variation, or self-symmetries (acknowledged in limitations) may break the approach. Robustness to these cases is not systematically studied.

The parametric restriction of the symmetry distribution estimator (moment-based matrix-Fisher / parameter fitting in Equation 4) limits the expressiveness of discoverable symmetries, which sits in some tension with the paper's framing of discovering arbitrary instance-level symmetry distributions.

The OOD pose detection application lacks comparison to any baseline anomaly-detection methods, so it is unclear whether the learned symmetry distributions are necessary or merely sufficient for this task.

Some experimental details (e.g., sensitivity to k other than a single MNIST ablation, behavior on datasets without class-clustered invariant spaces) are under-explored relative to the generality of the claims.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with the problem of instance-level (rather than dataset-level) symmetry discovery clearly motivated and nicely illustrated in Figures 1-3.

The core idea of correcting arbitrary canonical poses via Fréchet mean normalization is sensible, interpretable, and technically coherent; Proposition 3.1 is stated carefully and the proof in Appendix B is plausible.
The application to SO(3) and matrix-Fisher distributions on molecular conformations (GEOM/QM9) is an interesting scaling of the problem beyond typical 2D rotation benchmarks.
Implementation details, hyperparameters, and training procedures are documented thoroughly in the appendix, and code is promised for release, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin. Proposition 3.1 essentially follows from the equivariance of the Fréchet mean under right-translation [21] plus the known consistency of the sample Fréchet mean [4]; the proof is a relatively direct composition of standard results dressed up as a 'main result'. The overall method is a post-hoc normalization step on top of an existing architecture (IE-AEs [48]), which limits novelty.

The evaluation is largely synthetic and circular. In both the MNIST/FashionMNIST experiments and the GEOM experiments, the 'ground truth' symmetry distributions are rotations injected by the authors themselves (uniform, Gaussian, and three fixed matrix-Fisher matrices). The paper's claim of discovering symmetries in 'real-world, large-scale 3D data' is overstated: the SO(3) pose variation is manufactured, and the estimator is evaluated against a parametric family it was designed to fit. No experiment demonstrates recovery of naturally occurring symmetry distributions.

Baselines are weak and incomplete. The only comparisons are against IE-AEs and SGMs, both of which produce unnormalized relative distributions and are thus structurally handicapped. Relevant related methods discussed in Section 4 (WSCNNs [43], VP G-CNNs [22], Urbano & Romero [42], Forestante et al. [18]) are dismissed textually but never empirically compared, even where comparisons seem feasible.

The method relies on a fragile pipeline of approximations: equivalence classes [x] are approximated by k-NN in a learned invariant space, pose distributions are restricted to a single parametric family (Gaussian / matrix-Fisher), and the class-mapping stage trains networks on pseudo-labels derived from these approximations. The sensitivity to k is acknowledged but only superficially analyzed; there is no ablation on the effect of invariant-space quality, cluster separation, or estimation error propagation.

The key assumption that the Fréchet mean defines a 'natural pose' is only valid for unimodal, well-separated distributions. Real symmetry distributions (e.g., multi-fold symmetric molecules, self-symmetric objects, which the authors themselves flag in Section 6) violate this, and the paper offers no empirical evidence of behavior in such cases.

The OOD pose-detection application (Section 5.3) reports AUC-ROC numbers with no baselines or comparisons whatsoever, making it impossible to judge significance. Similarly, Figure 6 results come with wide error bars and admitted underestimation for several classes, but no statistical analysis is provided.

Scale of evidence is modest: only two small image benchmarks and one molecular subset, with ground truth of the authors' own construction, are used to support the broad claims in the abstract ('first time', 'paving the way towards more flexible equivariant modeling').

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: discovering instance-level symmetry distributions without supervision, addressing a genuine limitation of both fixed-equivariance networks and existing symmetry discovery methods that inherit arbitrary canonical poses.

The proposed solution is elegant and principled: using the Fréchet mean as a canonical centroid on the group manifold to correct the arbitrary offset introduced by class-pose decomposition methods is a simple, theoretically grounded normalization step, formalized in Proposition 3.1 with a proof (Appendix B) covering both the noise-free translation relation and the noisy case via Wasserstein bounds.

The paper is honest about its relationship to prior work, particularly IE-AEs and SGMs, and clearly articulates why the arbitrary canonical pose is a fundamental obstacle for class-pose methods in symmetry discovery.

Experiments span both 2D images (rotated MNIST/FashionMNIST with controlled, class-dependent symmetry distributions) and a large-scale 3D setting (QM9/GEOM with SO(3) matrix-Fisher ground truths), the latter being, to my knowledge, the first demonstration of instance-level symmetry distribution discovery for 3D transformation groups.

The partial symmetry example (digits '6' vs '9') is a compelling demonstration that RECON can disambiguate cases where fully equivariant methods provably collapse, connecting to a well-known motivating example for partial equivariance.

Practical downstream utility is shown via OOD pose detection with competitive AUC-ROC values, and the paper includes a thoughtful limitations section identifying real weaknesses (parametric estimator restriction, a priori choice of G, k-NN class approximation).
Reproducibility appears strong: code is released, and the appendix provides unusually detailed implementation, data preparation, hyperparameter, and training-time information.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively incremental: the method is essentially a post-hoc Fréchet-mean centering of relative pose outputs on top of an existing architecture (IE-AE). The main algorithm (Algorithm 1) is straightforward, and the novelty rests mostly on identifying the canonical-pose offset problem and the normalization proposition rather than a new learning framework.

There is a gap between theory and practice: Proposition 3.1 assumes exact equivalence classes [x] defined via connected components in latent space, but in practice these are approximated with k-NN in the invariant embedding, and the paper provides limited analysis of how latent-space clustering errors propagate into symmetry estimation errors beyond a small k-sensitivity plot on MNIST.

Baselines and comparisons are limited. The method is primarily compared against IE-AE and SGM (the latter only qualitatively in distribution plots); there is no direct quantitative comparison with other symmetry discovery approaches (e.g., Forestano et al., Urbano & Romero, WSCNNs, VP-G-CNNs), making it hard to gauge the contribution relative to the field. The OOD detection results in Section 5.3 report AUCs with no competing baselines at all.

Evaluation metrics are largely self-defined (MSE between fitted matrix-Fisher parameters, MAE of predicted symmetry parameters), and there is no downstream task demonstrating that recovered symmetry distributions improve task performance (e.g., partially equivariant network design), which is the motivating long-term goal stated in the introduction.

A non-trivial fraction of molecules (~20% with MSE > 800 in Fig. 7) shows substantial prediction errors, and the explanation for these failures remains speculative ('limited conformer sampling or mixed symmetries') without deeper analysis.

The notion of 'natural pose' is data-dependent (centered at the Fréchet mean of observed poses), which is sensible statistically but means the canonical orientation reflects the majority pose in the data rather than any semantically meaningful orientation; the paper could discuss this more critically, and the approach may struggle with strongly multimodal or symmetric pose distributions where the Fréchet mean is non-unique or unrepresentative.

Scope is confined to rotation groups (SO(2), SO(3)) with parametric (uniform/Gaussian/matrix-Fisher) ground-truth distributions; the claim of generality to 'any distribution over a Lie group' is not empirically validated for non-unimodal or discrete distributions.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: correcting the arbitrary canonical poses of class-pose decomposition methods (e.g., IE-AEs, SGMs) is a genuine limitation of prior symmetry-discovery work, and RECON addresses it with an elegant, architecture-agnostic fix (Fréchet-mean right-multiplication).

Theoretical grounding is provided: Proposition 3.1 (with a reasonably careful proof in Appendix B) establishes Wasserstein convergence of the normalized distribution, and Proposition B.2 gives a right-translation invariance property of the anomaly score. The robust Tukey-Fréchet mean extension is well motivated and illustrated (Appendix C).

Experiments go beyond the typical 2D-only setting: synthetic SO(2) benchmarks (MNIST/FashionMNIST with known per-class symmetry distributions) plus a large-scale SO(3) GEOM-QM9 molecular experiment — the first 3D extension of instance-level symmetry discovery — with quantitative MSE evaluation and useful diagnostics (hit-rate analysis of equivalence classes, error-regime visualizations).

Two practically relevant downstream applications are demonstrated: OOD pose detection (consistent AUC-ROC gains over IE-AE across three datasets) and test-time canonicalization granting group invariance to frozen pre-trained models without retraining, with substantial accuracy improvements (e.g., 66.9% -> 92.94% on rotated MNIST) and a clear upper-bound reference.

Limitations are honestly discussed (reliance on instance-level class-pose decomposition, difficulties on natural multi-object scenes), and implementation/reproducibility details (hyperparameters, training schedules, hardware) are thorough, with code promised for release.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is relatively simple: the normalization is essentially a Fréchet (circular) mean over k-NN neighbors' relative poses followed by a right-multiplication. This is a post-hoc correction built entirely on top of the existing IE-AE backbone, and is close in spirit to the preliminary workshop work of Urbano & Romero (2024); the delta over that work should be more sharply delineated.

Evaluation is largely on synthetic/controlled symmetry settings: ground-truth symmetries are injected by the authors (per-class rotation distributions on MNIST/FashionMNIST; synthetic matrix-Fisher rotations on GEOM-QM9). There is no experiment on naturally occurring, unengineered symmetries, so real-world generality of the 'instance-specific symmetry distribution' claim is not directly tested.

Baselines are limited: comparisons are essentially IE-AE (uncentered variant of the same backbone) and qualitative references to SGM. No head-to-head quantitative comparison with SGM (the most closely related method) or with other symmetry-learning methods (Augerino, Partial G-CNNs, VP G-CNNs, WSCNNs), even if those methods target different goals.

Several modeling choices are heuristic and under-ablated: k=25 nearest neighbors chosen empirically (and only ablated on MNIST), parametric families for Θ (uniform/matrix-Fisher) restrict expressiveness, and the Tukey-Fréchet mean's sensitivity to the threshold c and its benefit on the actual benchmarks (vs. classical Fréchet) are not evaluated empirically.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., 'robustness to conformational complexity' is argued from absence of correlation (r=0.149 hit-rate trend; Fig. 12 correlations), and the equivalence-class definition relies on informal connected-proximity reasoning that is only approximated by k-NN in practice.

The problem setup assumes the symmetry group G is fixed a priori and that a single global symmetry distribution per class exists; multimodal/mixed symmetry cases (where the paper itself shows the Fréchet mean fails) are handled only qualitatively and not tested on the benchmarks.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: class-pose decomposition methods (IE-AEs, SGMs) produce arbitrary, often out-of-distribution canonical poses, and the proposed Fréchet-mean-based right-multiplication correction is a clean, architecture-agnostic fix.

Proposition 3.1 is backed by a reasonably careful proof (Appendix B) with explicit assumptions and convergence in Wasserstein distance, and the robust Tukey-Fréchet extension for multimodal distributions is a sensible, well-motivated addition (Appendix C with simulations).

The empirical scope is broader than much prior work: 2D images plus a large-scale 3D molecular experiment (GEOM-QM9), with useful applications (OOD pose detection with AUC-ROC gains, and test-time canonicalization improving frozen pre-trained models without retraining).

The paper is generally well written, with clear problem setup, honest limitations section, ablations (k-NN size, equivalence class quality via hit rate), and implementation details sufficient for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is quite simple: centering the distribution of predicted relative poses by right-multiplying with the inverse of an empirical Fréchet mean. This is a modest post-hoc correction on top of an existing backbone (IE-AE), and the novelty is incremental relative to the class-pose decomposition literature the paper builds on; the Tukey-Fréchet mean is a direct application of known robust M-estimators.

The headline claim of unsupervised 'symmetry discovery' is evaluated in a largely synthetic regime: ground-truth symmetry distributions (uniform/Gaussian rotations in MNIST/FashionMNIST; matrix-Fisher distributions on GEOM) are injected by the authors themselves. There is no experiment demonstrating discovery of naturally occurring, unknown symmetries in real data, which weakens the central claim of the paper.

Baselines are weak and narrow: the main quantitative comparisons are against the IE-AE backbone (and SGM only qualitatively via figures). Key alternative baselines are missing, e.g., test-time augmentation/rotation averaging for the canonicalization experiments, existing symmetry-discovery or partial-equivariance methods (Augerino, Partial G-CNNs, VP G-CNNs, WSCNNs), or simple heuristics for canonicalization. Without these, the significance of the reported gains (e.g., 92.94% vs. a 98.84% perfect-canonicalization upper bound) is hard to judge.

Several theoretical assumptions are strong and their practical impact is underexplored: near-zero, small-variance noise ε, continuity of ψ on a compact domain, and equivalence classes defined by connected proximity in the invariant latent space. In practice classes are approximated by k-NN with a hand-tuned k=25, and the theory–practice gap is acknowledged but not quantified beyond one MAE-vs-k plot.

The 3D experiment reports per-molecule MSE against matrix-Fisher parameters without a clear sense of scale or a baseline; the claim that '80% of molecules fall within accurate predictions (approx. MSE < 800 based on visualizations)' is unconvincing, as the threshold is chosen by visual inspection and no competing method is evaluated.

The identity-centered 'natural pose' definition via the Fréchet mean is intuitively appealing but not always well justified: for symmetric or multimodal distributions the notion of a unique natural pose is contested, and the robust estimator introduces a sensitive hyperparameter c (set to π/4 for SO(2), with no systematic guidance for SO(3)).

The method inherits fundamental limitations of the class-pose backbone (whole-scene group action, difficulty with multi-object scenes), which the authors candidly acknowledge; this substantially narrows the practical impact of the claimed applications to realistic vision settings.

Some claims appear overstated: 'for the first time extend symmetry discovery to 3D groups' downplays the extensive 3D equivariance-learning literature, and the drop-in, retrain-free framing of test-time canonicalization is only validated on rotated MNIST/FashionMNIST and one GCN on GEOM-QM9.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and well-motivated problem: class-pose decomposition methods (IE-AEs, SGMs) learn canonical representations with arbitrary orientations, which corrupts relative-pose distributions and produces out-of-distribution canonicalizations.

The proposed solution is simple, elegant, and general: estimating the Fréchet mean of relative poses within a class and right-multiplying by its inverse. This is architecture-agnostic and theoretically grounded (Proposition 3.1 with a Wasserstein-convergence proof, plus a right-translation-invariance result for the OOD score).

The robust Tukey-Fréchet mean extension is a thoughtful addition, addressing the well-known failure of the Fréchet mean on multimodal distributions (e.g., bimodal on SO(2)), with supporting simulations.
The paper extends symmetry discovery beyond 2D images to 3D/SO(3) on a large-scale molecular dataset (GEOM-QM9, ~220k conformers, 2,221 classes), which is a genuine expansion over prior 2D-only work.

Two practical downstream applications are demonstrated convincingly: OOD pose detection (consistent AUC-ROC gains over IE-AE across three datasets) and test-time canonicalization granting group invariance to frozen pre-trained models without retraining — a useful, adoption-friendly capability.

Reproducibility is good: extensive implementation details (architectures, hyperparameters, seeds, hardware), ablations (k-NN neighborhood size, equivalence-class hit-rate analysis, uncentered vs. centered scoring), and a promised code release.
The limitation section is candid (instance-level vs. object-level symmetry, reliance on class-pose backbones, reliance on nearest-neighbor class approximations).
weaknesses: Limited quantitative baselines: the most closely related method (SGM, Allingham et al. 2024) is only compared qualitatively (Figures 2, 5b) and is absent from the quantitative symmetry-recovery and OOD-detection tables. Other instance-level symmetry methods (e.g., VP G-CNNs) are discussed but not empirically compared, weakening the claim of superiority.

The core contribution is conceptually a mean-centering/alignment correction on top of an existing backbone (IE-AE). The theoretical result relies on strong assumptions (continuous ψ on compact X, near-zero noise, correct class identification), while practice uses a heuristic k-NN surrogate for the theoretically defined equivalence classes; the gap between theory and practice is acknowledged but not formally bridged.

Evaluation is largely on synthetically injected symmetries (uniform/Gaussian rotations on MNIST/FashionMNIST; matrix-Fisher rotations on GEOM-QM9). The 'real-world' claim for the 3D experiment is tempered by the fact that ground-truth pose distributions are artificially imposed.

The test-time canonicalization gains, while clear, remain far from the perfect-canonicalization upper bound (e.g., 92.94% vs. 98.84% on MNIST), and the pipeline requires training three additional components (IE-AE + Θ + Λ), which limits the 'drop-in' narrative.
Pseudo-label training of Θ and Λ from Algorithm 1 introduces a circularity/error-propagation concern (biases in Γ and θ estimates become supervision), which is not quantitatively analyzed.

Minor writing issues: several typos and grammatical slips ('a promising foundations lies', 'the the QM9'), and some figure/text density issues; the Wasserstein bound in the proof is loose (a constant ω(ε′) upper bound over the full coupling), which is acceptable but undercuts the precision of the theoretical contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: arbitrary canonical poses in class-pose decomposition methods lead to out-of-distribution canonicalizations and non-comparable, arbitrarily shifted relative-pose distributions. The proposed fix (right-multiplying relative poses by the inverse of the empirical Fréchet mean) is simple, principled, and architecture-agnostic.

Proposition 3.1 provides a clean consistency guarantee, and the proof in Appendix B is careful: it connects noise-induced perturbations of ψ to Wasserstein closeness via uniform continuity, leverages established results on Fréchet mean equivariance and consistency (Karcher; Afsari; Aveni & Mukherjee), and the right-translation invariance result (Prop. B.2) justifies the OOD scoring scheme.

The paper validates across 2D images and large-scale, real-world 3D molecular data (GEOM-QM9, ~175k samples), which goes beyond the 2D-only settings of most prior symmetry-discovery work. The evaluation covers symmetry recovery quality, OOD pose detection (AUC-ROC), and downstream test-time canonicalization accuracy.

The test-time canonicalization application is practically attractive: a plug-in, retrain-free module that grants group invariance to frozen backbones. It consistently outperforms the unsupervised IE-AE canonicalization (which actually degrades performance) and beats partially equivariant Partial G-CNNs, even surpassing a fully equivariant ESCNN on FashionMNIST.

The comparison against EquiAdapt is conducted under the same zero-shot setting (frozen predictor), making the supervision-free claim fair. Hyperparameter searches for baselines (Tables 4-5) are reported, reducing the risk of weak-baseline bias.

The limitations section is unusually honest and specific (mismatch of group action with object-local symmetries in natural scenes, reliance on latent-space class separation, parametric density families), and failure modes of the equivalence-class construction are analyzed quantitatively (hit-rate analysis, Figs. 11-13). Code and reproducibility statements are provided.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a relatively small delta on top of existing class-pose backbones (IE-AE, SGM): the normalization is a single right-translation by an inverse empirical Fréchet mean, and Proposition 3.1 is essentially a consistency statement assembled from standard Riemannian statistics results. The theoretical novelty is modest, and the practical contribution depends heavily on the backbone quality.

The experimental protocol for 'symmetry discovery' is largely self-referential: the ground-truth symmetry distributions are injected by the authors (uniform/Gaussian rotations on MNIST/FashionMNIST; three fixed matrix-Fisher distributions on GEOM), and the 'natural pose' is defined as the Fréchet mean of that injected distribution. This makes recovery of the injected distributions a somewhat synthetic benchmark; performance on genuinely arising, unknown symmetries in natural data is not demonstrated.

Downstream gains are mixed and sometimes modest: on GEOM-QM9 the test-time canonicalization improves accuracy only from 52.40% to 55.92%, far below the SE(3)-equivariant SEGNN (98.55%), and on MNIST RECON trails the supervised EquiAdapt (90.96% vs 94.52%). The claim of 'matching or outperforming' other canonicalizations holds, but the practical significance of the 3D gains is limited.

The method inherits strong assumptions from the class-pose backbone: it requires well-separated invariant latent clusters, a correctly prespecified group G, and a group action on the entire input. The authors acknowledge these restrict applicability to natural images and multi-object scenes, but this leaves the most practically relevant regime untested.

The Fréchet vs. Tukey-Fréchet estimator distinction is somewhat underexplored empirically in the main results; the robust variant is justified mainly through simulations on SO(2) (Fig. 8) and qualitative discussion (digit '8'), and the choice of the tuning constant c is not thoroughly ablated on the real datasets.

Some experimental details are spread thin: e.g., the FashionMNIST prediction-error metric (MAE of a distributional parameter in degrees) is less interpretable than density-level metrics, and the OOD labeling for GEOM relies on a hand-tuned likelihood threshold (τ=96) whose sensitivity is not analyzed.

strengths: The problem of arbitrary, training-dependent canonicals in class-pose decomposition methods is clearly identified and well motivated; the proposed Fréchet-mean-based orientation normalization is simple, architecture-agnostic, and practically useful.

The paper is technically careful: Proposition 3.1 and Prop. B.2 are stated precisely, with proofs in the appendix that correctly handle the noise model via a Wasserstein-distance argument and consistency of the sample Fréchet mean.

Good breadth of evaluation: 2D images (MNIST, FashionMNIST) and 3D molecular data (GEOM-QM9), covering symmetry recovery, OOD pose detection, and test-time canonicalization, with baselines (IE-AE, EquiAdapt, Partial G-CNNs, ESCNN/SEGNN) and ablations (neighborhood size k, hit-rate analysis of the equivalence classes, Tukey-Fréchet vs Fréchet).

The downstream test-time canonicalization is a genuinely practical contribution: it improves frozen pretrained backbones without retraining or supervision, sometimes surpassing fully equivariant architectures (FashionMNIST), and the limitations section is honest about the object-centric mismatch in natural scenes.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method is essentially a right-multiplication by the inverse empirical Fréchet mean of the relative poses. Proposition 3.1 follows fairly directly from continuity of ψ and known consistency results for Fréchet means; the Tukey-Fréchet extension is a straightforward adaptation of existing robust M-estimators. The paper reads more as a well-executed engineering add-on to IE-AEs/SGM than a fundamental methodological advance.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: all experiments use rotation groups (SO(2)/SO(3)) with synthetic, author-constructed ground-truth symmetry distributions on small/simple datasets (MNIST, FashionMNIST, QM9). No evidence is given for the method on natural image datasets or on more complex/realistic symmetry regimes, which weakens the generality claims in the abstract.

The test-time canonicalization results are mixed: on MNIST, RECON (90.96%) clearly trails EquiAdapt (94.52%) which uses supervision, and both fall short of a supervised equivariant classifier (94.59–94.72%). The claimed advantages rest on being unsupervised and plug-and-play, but the practical gain over EquiAdapt is debatable; on GEOM-QM9 even RECON's best result (55.92%) is far from the equivariant SEGNN upper bound (98.55%).

The 'natural pose' definition (Fréchet mean at identity) is somewhat arbitrary and assumption-dependent: it presumes the generating model s = ρX(g)γ[x] + εs with identity-centered µ[x] and small, zero-mean noise. Deviations from this generative assumption (heavy noise, multimodal poses not separated enough for the Tukey correction, structured non-group variation) are analyzed only partially.

Performance depends sensitively on the quality of the pretrained class-pose backbone and the k-NN approximation of equivalence classes; failure modes (inter-class latent overlap) are acknowledged but only mitigated in discussion, not empirically in the main results.

Several quantities in the evaluation (matrix-Fisher parameters, per-class symmetry parameters) are self-defined proxies rather than externally validated metrics, making it hard to assess real-world significance of the symmetry discovery claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: unsupervised, instance-level discovery of pose/symmetry distributions, which most prior symmetry-discovery methods (LieGG, LieGAN, Partial G-CNNs, WSCNNs) do not expose.

The core technical contribution (canonical orientation normalization via the Fréchet mean of relative poses) is simple, elegant, and theoretically grounded: Proposition 3.1 provides a Wasserstein-convergence argument with a proof in the appendix, and the robust Tukey-Fréchet variant addresses the well-known multimodality failure mode of Fréchet means with supporting simulations (Fig. 8).

Evaluation goes beyond the typical 2D-only setting: symmetry recovery is validated on MNIST/FashionMNIST with per-class ground-truth rotation distributions and on a large-scale, real-world 3D dataset (GEOM-QM9, ~175k samples, 2,221 molecule classes) with SO(3) matrix-Fisher ground truths.

Two concrete downstream applications are demonstrated: OOD pose detection (with an ablation vs. uncentered baselines, Prop. B.2) and a plug-and-play test-time canonicalization layer that improves frozen pre-trained classifiers without retraining, compared against EquiAdapt and reference equivariant architectures.

The manuscript is well written and organized, with thorough appendices (implementation details, hyperparameter searches, equivalence-class/hit-rate analysis, computational analysis, honest failure-mode discussion), and includes reproducibility and ethics statements with public code.
weaknesses: The novelty of the core idea is moderate: right-translating a distribution to center it at a Fréchet mean is a standard statistical operation; the contribution is its combination with class-pose backbones and its applications rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. This should be more explicitly acknowledged.

The theoretical result rests on idealized assumptions that may be far from practice: continuous ψ on a compact domain, small bounded noise ε', Fréchet-mean Lipschitzness within Karcher convexity balls, and exact class recovery — while in practice classes are approximated by k-NN (k=10–25), which the theory does not cover. The gap between Proposition 3.1 and the actual algorithm deserves discussion.

Ground-truth symmetries are synthetically injected (per-class rotations sampled from known distributions), so the 'discovery' evaluation measures recovery of known augmentations rather than naturally occurring symmetries. GEOM conformers are also pre-aligned and RMSD-filtered, which simplifies the problem relative to realistic conditions.

Quantitative comparison against the most closely related method, SGM (Allingham et al., 2024), appears limited to qualitative arguments (Figs. 1, 2, 5b) and citations of its known limitations; a direct head-to-head symmetry-discovery comparison is missing.

Test-time canonicalization gains are modest in the harder 3D setting (55.92% vs. 52.96% EquiAdapt, vs. a 96.4% perfect-canonicalization upper bound), and the method remains below the SE(2)-equivariant ESCNN on MNIST (90.96% vs. 94.59%), tempering the practical-impact claims. GEOM canonicalization training also reportedly takes days on an A100.

The method's quality depends heavily on the backbone: the claimed 'instance-level' granularity actually degrades to class-level k-NN neighborhoods, and the limitations section candidly notes the method does not extend to scenes/multi-object or in-the-wild settings, which narrows the scope of the contribution.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'robust symmetry discovery' and 'natural pose' framing; the natural pose is defined only implicitly via the (Tukey-)Fréchet mean, and results like the ~20% high-error regime on GEOM-QM9 are attributed to 'other sources' without full diagnosis.
